source_text: Ceterum rettulimus supra de locorum condicione, quod non per semetipsa nos inquinent, sed per ea quae illic geruntur, per quae, simul inquinamentum combiberunt, tunc etiam in alteros respuunt. uiderit ergo, ut diximus, principalis titulus, idololatria; reliquas ipsarum rerum qualitates contra ut dei omnes feramus. deus praecepit spiritum sanctum, utpote pro naturae suae bono tenerum et delicatum, tranquillitate et lenitate et quiete et pace tractare, non furore, non bile, non ira, non, dolore inquietare. huic quomodo cum spectaculis poterit conuenire? omne enim spectaculum sine concussione spiritus non est. ubi enim Uoluptas, ibi et studium, per quod scilicet uoluptas sapit; ubi studium, ibi et aemulatio, per quam studium sapit. porro et ubi aemulatio, ibi et furor et bilis et ira et dolor et cetera ex his, quae cum his non conpetunt disciplinae. nam et si qui modeste et probe spectaculis fruitur pro dignitatis uel aetatis uel etiam naturae suae condicione, non tamen immobilis animi est et sine tacita spiritus passione. nemo ad uoluptatem uenit sine affectu, nemo affectum sine casibus suis patitur. ipsi casus incitamenta sunt affectus. ceterum si cessat affectus, nulla est uoluptas, et est reus iam ille uanitatis eo conueniens, ubi nihil consequitur. sed puto, [autem] etiam uanitas extranea est nobis. quid quod et ipse se iudicat inter eos positus, quorum se simul nolens utique detestatorem confitetur? nobis satis non est, si ipsi nihil tale facimus, nisi et talia factitantibus non conferamur. si furem, inquit, uidebas, concurrebas cum eo. utinam ne in saeculo quidem simul cum illis moraremur. sed tamen in saecularibus separamur, quia saeculum dei est, saecularia autem diaboli.
thought_title: The passions of the shows are incompatible with the Holy Spirit
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his argument that the shows must be rejected because they excite passions contrary to Christian discipline, even apart from their idolatrous origins.
pass_a_gloss: But we have related above about the condition of the places, that they do not defile us through themselves, but through the things which are done there, through which, once they have drunk in the defilement, then they also spit it back upon others. Let the principal title, idolatry, see to it, as we have said; let us bring the remaining qualities of the things themselves against all of them as gods. God commanded the Holy Spirit, inasmuch as it is tender and delicate by the good of its nature, to be handled with tranquillity and gentleness and quiet and peace, not to be disturbed with fury, not with bile, not with anger, not with grief. How will this be able to agree with the shows? For every show is not without a shaking of the spirit. For where there is pleasure, there also is eagerness, through which, of course, pleasure has its savor; where there is eagerness, there also is rivalry, through which eagerness has its savor. Furthermore, where there is rivalry, there also is fury and bile and anger and grief and the rest of these things, which together with these are not suitable for discipline. For even if anyone enjoys the shows modestly and uprightly according to the condition of his rank or age or even of his nature, nevertheless he is not of an unmoved mind and without a silent passion of the spirit. No one comes to pleasure without feeling, no one suffers feeling without its own falls. The falls themselves are incitements of feeling. But if feeling ceases, there is no pleasure, and that man is already guilty of vanity by going there, where he obtains nothing. But I think that vanity also is foreign to us. What of the fact that he also judges himself, placed among those whose detester he confesses himself to be, unwillingly of course? It is not enough for us, if we ourselves do nothing of such a kind, unless we also do not associate with those who do such things. If you saw a thief, it says, you ran together with him. Would that we did not linger together with them even in the world. But nevertheless in worldly things we are separated, because the world is God's, but worldly things are the devil's.

choices.term: uiderit ergo, ut diximus, principalis titulus, idololatria
choices.english: Let the principal title, idolatry, see to it, as we have said
choices.why: Preserves the legal metaphor of 'title' as the primary charge already established, and the jussive force of 'uiderit' as 'let it see to it'.
rejected: Let the principal charge, idolatry, be enough

choices.term: reliquas ipsarum rerum qualitates contra ut dei omnes feramus
choices.english: let us bring the remaining qualities of the things themselves against all of them as gods
choices.why: Keeps the awkward 'ut dei omnes' as 'as gods' to show Tertullian's compressed expression: the qualities themselves are brought as charges against the gods.
rejected: let us bring the remaining qualities of the things themselves against all the gods

choices.why: Literal rendering of 'concussio' as 'shaking' preserves the physical metaphor of disturbance that Tertullian applies to the Holy Spirit.
Keeps the gustatory metaphor of 'sapit' (tastes, has flavor) which Tertullian uses to link pleasure to eagerness.
Literal 'falls' preserves the sense of mishaps or accidents that befall feeling, and the reflexive 'suis'.

choices.term: si furem, inquit, uidebas, concurrebas cum eo
choices.english: If you saw a thief, it says, you ran together with him
choices.why: Keeps the impersonal 'inquit' as 'it says' to mark the scriptural quotation without naming the source, and the literal 'ran together with'.
rejected: If you saw a thief, you joined him

pass_b_english: I have already discussed the condition of the places: they do not defile us by themselves, but by what is done in them. Once they have drunk in that defilement, they then spit it back onto others. So let the principal title, idolatry, see to it, as we have said. Let us bring the remaining qualities of those things against all the gods.

God has commanded that the Holy Spirit—tender and delicate as it is by the goodness of its nature—be handled with tranquility, gentleness, quiet, and peace, not disturbed by frenzy, bile, anger, or grief. How can this possibly agree with the shows? Every show involves a shaking of the spirit. Where there is pleasure, there is also eagerness, through which pleasure has its savor. Where there is eagerness, there is also rivalry, through which eagerness has its savor. And where there is rivalry, there is frenzy, bile, anger, grief, and the rest of what follows from these—none of which is suitable for discipline.

Even if someone enjoys the shows modestly and uprightly, according to his rank, age, or natural disposition, his mind is still moved, and not without a silent passion of the spirit. No one comes to pleasure without feeling; no one suffers feeling without its own lapses. Those very lapses are the incitements of feeling. If feeling ceases, there is no pleasure, and the man is already guilty of vanity by going where he gains nothing. But I think vanity too is foreign to us.

What of the fact that he judges himself by sitting among those whose detester he confesses himself to be, even unwillingly? It is not enough for us if we ourselves do no such thing, unless we also do not associate with those who do such things. "If you saw a thief," it says, "you ran together with him." Would that we did not even linger in the world with them! But still, in worldly matters we are separated, because the world is God's, but worldly things are the devil's.
